title: Fuel regulator for gas engines (multi-agent)
description: a fuel regulator for gaseous-fueled engines
reference_excerpt: The product in question is an N-LPR series regulator designed specifically for gaseous-fueled engines. It functions as a self-operating valve that utilizes engine vacuum to control the flow of fuel to the engine. The classification under HTSUS 8481.80.9015 is appropriate as it pertains to regulator valves that are self-operating and are used for controlling variables such as temperature, pressure, flow, and liquid level. The ruling confirms that this specific type of regulator falls under the category of self-operating valves, thus justifying the assigned HTS code.

text: {"heading":"8481","best_code":"8481.80.90.15","argument":"A fuel regulator for gaseous-fueled engines is a valve-type appliance that regulates fuel pressure and flow. Heading 8481 covers 'Taps, cocks, valves and similar appliances, for pipes, boiler shells, tanks, vats or the like, including pressure-reducing valves and thermostatically controlled valves.' A fuel regulator is a self-operating regulator valve that controls pressure—a core function within the scope of heading 8481. The product is a complete, functional assembly (not a part), made of metal, designed to regulate gaseous fuel delivery to internal combustion engines. Chapter 84 notes do not exclude it. The best 10-digit code is 8481.80.90.15 ('Regulator valves, self-operating, for controlling variables such as temperature, pressure, flow and liquid level'), which directly describes a self-operating pressure regulator. Ruling H262289 (in force) examined a compressed natural gas fuel tank system and confirmed that a high-pressure regulator reducing gas pressure for engine delivery falls within heading 8481. text: {"heading":"8407","best_code":"8407.90.9010","argument":"A fuel regulator for gaseous-fueled engines is a part suitable for use solely or principally with spark-ignition or compression-ignition internal combustion piston engines. Heading 8407 covers spark-ignition reciprocating or rotary internal combustion piston engines, and heading 8409 covers parts suitable for use solely or principally with the engines of heading 8407 or 8408. However, the user requests classification under heading 8407 itself. A fuel regulator is a component that regulates fuel pressure and flow—it is not itself an engine. Under GRI 1, a fuel regulator does not meet the description of heading 8407, which names 'engines.' The regulator is a part or accessory of an engine, not an engine. Heading 8409 is the proper heading for parts suitable for use solely or principally with engines of heading 8407 or 8408. For gaseous-fueled engines (natural gas or LP gas), the best code under 8409 would be 8409.99.99 (Other parts for other engines). However, if the regulator is for a spark-ignition gaseous engine, 8409.91.99 would apply. Since the product description specifies 'gaseous-fueled engines' without limiting to spark-ignition only, 8409.99.99 is the most appropriate. Nevertheless, arguing for heading 8407 as requested: a fuel regulator could theoretically be viewed as an incomplete or unfinished component that has the essential character of a gaseous-fueled engine under GRI 2(a), but this is a weak argument because a regulator alone does not constitute an engine or have the essential character of one. The regulator is a control component, not the prime mover. Heading 8407 text does not include regulators; they are accessories. memo.argument: A fuel regulator for gaseous-fueled engines is a part suitable for use solely or principally with spark-ignition or compression-ignition internal combustion piston engines. Heading 8407 covers spark-ignition reciprocating or rotary internal combustion piston engines, and heading 8409 covers parts suitable for use solely or principally with the engines of heading 8407 or 8408. However, the user requests classification under heading 8407 itself. A fuel regulator is a component that regulates fuel pressure and flow—it is not itself an engine. Under GRI 1, a fuel regulator does not meet the description of heading 8407, which names 'engines.' The regulator is a part or accessory of an engine, not an engine. Heading 8409 is the proper heading for parts suitable for use solely or principally with engines of heading 8407 or 8408. For gaseous-fueled engines (natural gas or LP gas), the best code under 8409 would be 8409.99.99 (Other parts for other engines). However, if the regulator is for a spark-ignition gaseous engine, 8409.91.99 would apply. Since the product description specifies 'gaseous-fueled engines' without limiting to spark-ignition only, 8409.99.99 is the most appropriate. Nevertheless, arguing for heading 8407 as requested: a fuel regulator could theoretically be viewed as an incomplete or unfinished component that has the essential character of a gaseous-fueled engine under GRI 2(a), but this is a weak argument because a regulator alone does not constitute an engine or have the essential character of one. The regulator is a control component, not the prime mover. Heading 8407 text does not include regulators; they are accessories. The argument for 8407 fails under GRI 1 because the heading text does not cover parts or accessories—only engines themselves.
exclusions_against: Heading 8407 covers only 'Spark-ignition reciprocating or rotary internal combustion piston engines'—the text does not include parts, accessories, or regulators. A fuel regulator is not an engine.
Chapter 84 Note 1 does not exclude parts from chapter 84, but GRI 1 requires that the heading text itself must cover the article. Heading 8407 text is limited to engines, not their parts.
Section XVI Note 1 does not exclude parts and accessories of machinery from section XVI, but heading 8407 specifically names only engines, not their components.

classification.rationale: A fuel regulator for gaseous-fueled engines functions as a self-operating pressure-reducing/regulating valve, squarely within the heading 8481 text covering 'taps, cocks, valves and similar appliances... including pressure-reducing valves.' Section XVI Note 2(a) mandates that parts which are themselves goods described by a heading of chapter 84 (such as valves) be classified under that heading rather than as engine parts under 8409, so the 8409 argument fails despite being facially plausible. Heading 8407 is rejected because it covers only engines, not components. In-force rulings H262289 and N358644 support classifying gas fuel-system regulator/valve components under heading 8481, and GRI 6 places the article in the specific statistical line 8481.80.90.15 for self-operating regulator valves.
